1: # BMW Product Management Challenge: Assignment Specification & Requirements Guide
2: 
3: **Challenge:** AI for Product Decision Making  
4: **Host:** BMW Group Product Management  
5: **Scope Focus:** Automotive Product Development Process — Steps 1 & 2 (Market Research & Product Planning to Gate G1 Concept Freeze)  
6: **Target Derivatives:** BMW 1 Series (F70), BMW 5 Series (G60/G68), BMW 7 Series (G70), and Future Successor Lines (Neue Klasse Architecture)  
7: **Target Markets:** Europe (EU), United States (US), China (CN), and Rest of World (RoW)  
8: 
9: ---
10: 
11: ## 1. Executive Summary & Mission Statement
12: 
13: Modern automotive product management requires synthesizing billions of fragmented market signals, customer reviews, warranty reports, competitor actions, and strategic corporate roadmaps into a coherent, customer-facing product specification. Today, this process spans approximately **two years** per vehicle generation and is predominantly manual, fragmented, and vulnerable to subjective bias.
14: 
15: ### The Mission
16: Develop an AI-powered, human-in-the-loop enterprise application that:
17: 1. **Ingests Heterogeneous Data**: Combines internal BMW customer feedback, quantitative satisfaction surveys, vehicle equipment catalogs, and strategic corporate reports.
18: 2. **Extracts Actionable Signals**: Discovers recurring complaints, unmet customer needs, competitor advantages, and emerging market trends, each strictly linked to originating evidence.
19: 3. **Derives SMART Product Requirements**: Formulates clear, customer-facing, realistic, and measurable requirements adhering to SMART criteria.
20: 4. **Prioritizes with Explainable Logic**: Applies an objective, transparent, multi-factor scoring methodology that balances customer value, regional volume impact, corporate strategy, and implementation complexity.
21: 5. **Keeps the Product Manager Firmly in the Loop**: Enables the PM to review, approve, reject, modify, or challenge requirements, rationales, and underlying evidence.
22: 6. **Maintains a Forensic Audit Trail**: Chronologically logs every system derivation, PM intervention, score override, and decision rationale to guarantee end-to-end governance.
23: 
24: ---
25: 
26: ## 2. Automotive Product Development Process Alignment
27: 
28: BMW management explicitly bounded the scope of this challenge to **Steps 1 and 2** of the 13-stage Automotive Product Development Lifecycle:
29: 
30: ```mermaid
31: flowchart TD
32:     subgraph Step1["Step 1: Market Research & Needs Analysis"]
33:         A1["Activities: Market Research, Customer Insights, Competitor Benchmarking, Trend Analysis"]
34:         A2["Deliverables: Market Opportunity Report, Customer Needs Document, Target Segments"]
35:         G0["Decision Gate: G0 — Project Approval"]
36:         A1 --> A2 --> G0
37:     end
38: 
39:     subgraph Step2["Step 2: Product Planning (Core App Focus)"]
40:         B1["Activities: Define Product Vision, Positioning, SMART Feature Prioritization, Trade-off Resolution"]
41:         B2["Deliverables: Product Plan, Project Charter, Prioritized Requirement List, Initial Business Sizing"]
42:         G1["Decision Gate: G1 — Concept Freeze"]
43:         B1 --> B2 --> G1
44:     end
45: 
46:     subgraph Step3["Steps 3 to 13: Concept to Continuous Feedback"]
47:         C1["G2 Feasibility -> G3 Design Freeze -> ... -> G9 SOP -> Step 13 Market Feedback Loop"]
48:     end

50:     Step1 --> Step2 --> Step3

58: ### Boundary Definitions
59: * **In-Scope (Customer-Facing Product Attributes)**:
60:   * Interior comfort, ergonomics, and spatial packaging
61:   * Infotainment, operating system UX, and connected digital services
62:   * Climatization and thermal comfort controls
63:   * Driving experience and dynamic perception
64:   * Real-world charging UX and range perception
65:   * Equipment packaging, option bundling, and regional variant differentiation
66: * **Out-of-Scope**:
67:   * Regulatory and homologation compliance (e.g., UNECE safety, emissions type approval)
68:   * Low-level component specifications and supplier engineering schematics
69:   * Detailed unit economics, factory tooling capex, and bill-of-materials pricing calculations (rough implementation complexity/effort sizing is utilized as a prioritization factor)
70: 
71: ---
72: 
73: ## 3. Data Ecosystem & Inputs Profile
74: 
75: The application processes four distinct tiers of heterogeneous data:
76: 
77: ```
78: BMW-Data/
79: ├── F70_feedback_hackathon.xlsx              # 4,076 rows (1 Series - UK, JP, SE, FR)
80: ├── G60_feedback_hackathon.xlsx              # 5,005 rows (5 Series - US, KR, GB, JP, SE)
81: ├── G70_feedback_hackathon.xlsx              # 4,690 rows (7 Series - US, KR, JP, GB, CA)
82: ├── F70_G60_G68_G70_customer_studies.xlsx    # Quantitative satisfaction studies (China, EU, US)
83: ├── sales_volumes.xlsx                       # Market deliveries (2024, 2025, 2030 projections)
84: ├── F70_OptionList.PDF                       # Official German equipment catalog & packaging (1er)
85: ├── G60_OptionList.PDF                       # Official German equipment catalog & packaging (5er)
86: ├── G70_OptionList.PDF                       # Official German equipment catalog & packaging (7er)
87: └── BMW_Group_Report_2025.pdf / Q-Deck       # 400-page strategic corporate & financial report
88: ```
89: 
90: ### Dataset Characteristics
91: 
92: | Dataset | Volume | Key Attributes | Strategic Value |
93: | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
94: | **Customer Feedback** | 13,771 rows | `ID`, `Country`, `Engine Type` (ICE, BEV, PHEV), `Feedback Type` (Likes, DTU, Defect, Wants), `Customer Feedback`, `Vfc Category` | Voice of the customer; ground-truth operational friction, ergonomics, and feature desires. |
95: | **Customer Studies** | Quantitative sheets | Likert ratings (US) & Mean satisfaction scores (CN vs. EU) across 15 vehicle systems | Macro-level customer satisfaction benchmarks; correlates qualitative text with quantitative validation. |
96: | **Sales Volumes** | 4 regions $\times$ 3 vehicle lines | Volumes for 2024, 2025, and 2030 projections across EU, US, China, and RoW | Objective volume weighting factor for prioritization formulas. |
97: | **Option Catalogs** | 3 German PDFs | Standard vs. optional equipment, option codes, bundle packages (Innovation, Travel, Comfort) | Grounds proposed requirements in realistic production packaging. |
98: | **Strategic Report Deck** | ~400 pages | Neue Klasse platform roadmap, R&D priorities, BEV delivery targets, digital software KPIs | Strategic validation layer; ties customer desires to BMW engineering investments. |
99: 
100: ---
101: 
102: ## 4. Evaluation Criteria & Scoring Rubric
103: 
104: The challenge will be judged on five primary criteria, with one critical guiding principle:
105: 
106: | Dimension | Weight | Key Evaluation Requirements |
107: | :--- | :---: | :--- |
108: | **Decision & Scoring Logic** | 25% | Quality, consistency, and mathematical explainability of prioritization. Clear demonstration of how evidence sources are weighted and combined, and how trade-offs and conflicting signals are resolved. |
109: | **Workflow & Human Decision-Making** | 20% | Completeness of the end-to-end workflow from raw findings to prioritized requirements. Clearly defined roles, decision gates, and boundaries between autonomous AI and mandatory human review. |
110: | **Traceability & Auditability** | 20% | Full backward lineage from every requirement and score back to originating quotes, surveys, and report slides. Complete, chronological, tamper-evident audit history of all approvals, edits, and rejections. |
111: | **Solution Quality, Usability & Feasibility** | 20% | Prototype UI/UX polish, usability for BMW Product Managers and engineering peers, realistic applicability in an enterprise automotive environment, and quality of SMART formulations. |
112: | **Innovation, Scalability & Business Impact** | 15% | Originality of approach, cross-derivative scalability (F70 $\to$ G60 $\to$ G70 $\to$ Neue Klasse), reduction in manual requirement definition cycle time, and prevention of costly late-stage engineering rework. |
113: 
114: ### The Winning Differentiator: "We Reward Honesty"
115: > **Direct Quote from BMW Challenge Evaluation Criteria:**  
116: > *"We reward honesty. Trustworthy AI acknowledges uncertainty. Show us where your app lacks evidence, encounters conflicting signals, or reaches uncertain conclusions, and how this is surfaced to the PM. Honest limitations are a strength, not a weakness."*
117: 
118: The application must include an explicit **Uncertainty & Evidence Confidence Index** that transparently highlights:
119: 1. Low sample size / weak empirical support
120: 2. Regional contradictions (e.g., EU Autobahn driver desires vs. China chauffeur comfort)
121: 3. Extrapolations based on forward-looking assumptions (e.g., 2030 battery/software tech) versus proven historical data
122: 
123: ---
124: 
125: ## 5. SMART Requirements Framework
126: 
127: BMW requirements must strictly comply with the **SMART** standard:
128: 
129: | SMART Dimension | Definition | Automotive Context |
130: | :--- | :--- | :--- |
131: | **Specific** | Concrete and unambiguous system or feature scope | Exact UI component, sensor, or interior system |
132: | **Measurable** | Objective engineering/UX KPIs & thresholds | Clear quantifiable metrics (e.g. latency $< 45\text{ms}$, 60 fps) |
133: | **Attainable** | Feasible within vehicle architecture & manufacturing | Compatible with platform packaging & wiring harness |
134: | **Relevant** | Meaningfully solves verified customer pain | Directly resolves top complaint or aligns with brand strategy |
135: | **Timely** | Explicit SOP target & vehicle milestone | SOP 2028 (LCI / Successor / Neue Klasse milestone) |
136: 
137: ### Benchmark Example: From Complaint to SMART Requirement
138: * **Raw Voice of Customer (`G70-0891`)**: *"Customer noted she would have chosen the Home theater screen, but it obstructs the view out the rear and BMW does not offer a camera/rear-view mirror screen."*
139: * **Unacceptable Requirement (Vague)**: *"Improve rear visibility when the theater screen is down."*
140: * **SMART Requirement (`REQ-G70-VIS-001`)**:
141:   * **Specific**: Full-display digital streaming rear-view mirror system utilizing an aerodynamic roof-mounted wide-angle camera feeding directly into the central rear-view mirror.
142:   * **Measurable**: End-to-end video latency $< 45\text{ ms}$; frame rate $\ge 60\text{ fps}$ at $1080\text{p}$; dynamic range $> 120\text{ dB}$ (headlight anti-glare); camera lens auto-defrosting and wash nozzle operational from $-30^\circ\text{C}$ to $+65^\circ\text{C}$.
143:   * **Attainable**: Integrates with the existing Neue Klasse roof shark-fin camera housing and high-speed automotive Ethernet backbone.
144:   * **Relevant**: Eliminates the #1 safety blocker preventing theater screen adoption; projected to increase Theater Screen package take-rate by 18%.
145:   * **Timely**: Targeted for SOP 2028 (G70 LCI / Neue Klasse Luxury derivative).
146:   * **Package Strategy**: Standard on i7 M70; optional in Innovation Package for base derivatives.
147: 
148: ---
149: 
150: ## 6. Key Mentors & Stakeholder Insights
151: 
152: 1. **Bene_BMW (Product Management Pain Points)**:
153:    * *Cross-Market Regional Balancing*: Preferences differ radically by climate, usage habits, and culture. A single global specification often fails in either Europe, the US, or China.
154:    * *Predecessor Feedback Cycles*: Capturing field insights from outgoing models (e.g., F70, G60, G70) and projecting them 3–5 years ahead into future vehicle architectures.
155:    * *2-Year Timeline*: Requirement prioritization is not a one-time script; it is a collaborative, iterative governance process over ~24 months.
156: 2. **ThomasFremuthBMW**:
157:    * Ground proposals in real evidence; maintain strict data hygiene (do not commit raw internal data to public repositories).
158: 3. **Sebastian_BMW & ThomasBMW**:
159:    * Scope is tightly focused on Steps 1 & 2 of the automotive development framework.
160: 
161: ---
162: 
163: ## 7. Required Deliverables Checklist
164: 
165: - [ ] **Working Application Prototype**: Demonstrable full-stack software ingesting the datasets and providing an interactive PM experience.
166: - [ ] **Structured Sample Requirements List**: Complete table with Unique ID, SMART Description, Evidence Links, Priority Score, Evidence Level, Uncertainties, and Decision Status.
167: - [ ] **End-to-End Workflow Definition**: Clear division between AI autonomous analysis and mandatory PM decision gates.
168: - [ ] **Traceable & Reconstructable Audit Trail**: Forensic record of all requirement changes, score overrides, timestamps, actors, and documented rationales.
169: - [ ] **Pitch Presentation Deck (3–5 min)**: Compelling narrative demonstrating real-world value, data grounding, and Trustworthy AI principles.

content.text:
## Overall assessment

**The concept is strong and feasible for five people using AI heavily over 10–12 hours. I would keep the ambition, but substantially revise the data model, scoring, evidence handling, and delivery schedule.**

The plan covers most of the rubric, particularly the PM cockpit, traceability, uncertainty, and G1 export. Its biggest weakness is that several capabilities are described more confidently than their implementation or evidence supports.

That matters because **65% of the judging weight is decision logic, workflow, and auditability**. A polished dashboard with questionable counts or invented SMART targets will lose to a slightly simpler application with defensible decisions.

I also inspected the actual spreadsheets. They reveal some important issues that are not apparent from the specification alone.

---

## 1. Critical discovery: the proposed feedback schema does not fit the data

The plan treats every spreadsheet row as an independent finding and uses the supplied feedback ID as its primary key.

However:

| Dataset | Spreadsheet rows | Distinct feedback IDs |
|---|---:|---:|
| F70 | 4,076 | 2,128 |
| G60 | 5,005 | 4,000 |
| G70 | 4,690 | 4,000 |
| **Total** | **13,771** | **10,128** |

Repeated IDs contain **the same customer text with different category/type annotations**. For example, one comment can have both a “Likes” annotation and a “Difficult to Use” annotation for different topics.

### Consequences

The proposed schema in `IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md:84` would:

- Reject repeated IDs, or overwrite annotations if implemented with upserts.
- Inflate signal frequency if spreadsheet rows are counted as separate comments.
- Lose the fact that one comment can contain multiple topics and opposing sentiments.
- Overstate evidence confidence through duplicated citations.

### Recommended change

Model these separately:

```text
Source document
  └── Source rows
        ├── Canonical feedback comment
        └── Imported topic/type annotations

Canonical feedback comment
  └── Extracted issue spans
        └── Signals
              └── Requirements
```

Concretely:

- Preserve all 13,771 source rows and their worksheet locations.
- Store the 10,128 distinct feedback IDs as canonical comments.
- Keep the multiple annotations attached to each comment.
- Count distinct comments **per signal**, rather than annotation rows.
- Do not describe distinct comments as distinct customers; the data does not establish that.

**This is the highest-priority correction before implementation starts.**

---

## 2. Regional analysis needs much stronger safeguards

The regional divergence feature is potentially your best differentiator, but the current examples assume evidence that is not established.

The actual data shows:

- **No China free-text feedback** in the three feedback workbooks.
- Around **90.2% of distinct G60 comments are US comments**.
- Around **94.8% of distinct G70 comments are US comments**.
- F70 feedback is primarily GB and Japan.
- F70 sales projections are **zero for US and China**.
- China 5 Series survey results concern **G68**, while European results concern **G60**.

### Why this matters

“China prefers touch-first controls” cannot be inferred from an aggregate HVAC satisfaction score. Likewise, a G68–G60 difference could reflect the derivative, equipment, or respondent mix—not just regional preference.

The app should distinguish:

| Situation | Appropriate interpretation |
|---|---|
| Explicit opposing customer preferences | Supported regional conflict |
| Different aggregate satisfaction scores | Regional satisfaction difference |
| Evidence in one region, absent elsewhere | Coverage gap |
| Different derivatives being compared | Comparison with derivative confounding |
| German equipment catalog applied to another market | Packaging assumption requiring validation |

### Recommended improvement

Make **coverage** a first-class part of the regional matrix:

```text
Region | Distinct comments | Survey coverage | Derivative | Supported findings | Gaps
```

Also define the country-to-sales-region mapping explicitly. The sales workbook labels “Europe” as `EU`; decide how GB, Norway, etc. map into that commercial region.

**A missing-evidence cell is valuable output. Do not fill it with an AI-generated regional preference.**

---

## 3. The prioritization formula needs revision

This is a major issue because scoring is the largest judging category.

### A. Customer value saturates almost immediately

The proposed formula is:

```text
min(10, 1.8 × log₂(signal_count + 1) + severity_bonus + Kano_weight)
```

For a “Defect” classified as “Must-Have”:

```text
8 comments → 1.8 × log₂(9) + 2 + 2.5 ≈ 10.21 → capped at 10
```

So eight comments and eight hundred comments receive the same customer-value score.

Even the lowest listed combination—“Wants” plus “Delighter”—reaches the cap at roughly 21 comments.

**Most meaningful signals will collapse to the same score.**

### B. Raw counts reflect collection bias

A higher count may mean more feedback was collected for that market or source. It does not necessarily mean the issue is more prevalent.

Show a distinct-comment mention rate within an appropriate cohort:

```text
Distinct comments mentioning issue
──────────────────────────────────
Distinct available comments in the relevant derivative/region/powertrain cohort
```

Label this **share of available feedback**, not percentage of vehicle owners affected.

### C. The complexity weight cannot change the ranking

In the current formula, `W_IC` multiplies the denominator for every requirement. Changing it rescales all scores equally; it does not change their ordering.

That makes an “effort importance” slider mathematically misleading.

Also, dividing by complexity means a level-1 task can receive five times the score of an otherwise identical level-5 task. That strongly favors easy improvements over important product decisions.

### Recommended scoring model

For the prototype, use a bounded weighted model:

```text
Priority = 100 × (
    w_customer × CustomerValue
  + w_reach    × AddressableReach
  + w_strategy × StrategicFit
  + w_effort   × EaseOfImplementation
)
```

All factors are normalized to `[0,1]`; weights sum to one.

An illustrative default is:

```text
Customer 40% | Reach 25% | Strategy 20% | Ease 15%
```

These are **PM policy choices**, not objectively correct constants.

Each factor should have a visible derivation:

- **Customer value:** issue severity, cohort mention rate, and relevant survey support.
- **Reach:** applicable projected volume, scoped by derivative, market, and powertrain where data supports it.
- **Strategic fit:** explicit rubric with cited strategy evidence.
- **Ease:** anchored effort categories with an estimation rationale.

Keep the normalization reference stable so adding a requirement does not unexpectedly rescale every existing score.

### High-value addition: ranking sensitivity

Show:

> “This requirement ranks #2 under the baseline and #6 under a China-focused scenario.”

Then explain which factor caused the movement. This makes the existing what-if feature much more compelling.

---

## 4. Replace citation-count confidence with claim-level evidence quality

The current ECI formula is understandable, but it has weak semantics.

Problems include:

- Fifty repeated or narrow-source comments can look more trustworthy than a smaller, well-supported finding.
- Missing category labels are treated as impurity in otherwise genuine customer evidence.
- A survey is counted as corroboration even when it measures a broader, different construct.
- “Survey score drop” implies a historical comparison that the supplied 2025 sheets do not establish.
- Regional disagreement is mixed with uncertainty, although two conflicting preferences can both be well evidenced.

There is another parsing trap: the US study’s **“Sample total = 1” means 100% of the distribution**, not one respondent. Do not infer respondent counts from it.

### Recommended structure

Keep a headline evidence index if useful, but expose its components:

1. **Support:** distinct comments and source diversity.
2. **Coverage:** relevant markets, derivatives, and powertrains represented.
3. **Corroboration:** whether another source measures the same issue.
4. **Inference burden:** inferred labels, architecture assumptions, proposed targets.
5. **Contradictions:** explicit opposing evidence.

Treat the index as an **evidence-quality rubric**, not a calibrated probability of correctness.

Most importantly, assess evidence per claim:

| Claim | Evidence status |
|---|---|
| Customers struggle to access HVAC controls | Supported by linked comments |
| A proposed interaction target is achievable | Requires feasibility validation |
| China prefers a different layout | Unverified unless explicitly evidenced |
| A package change increases take-rate by 18% | Unsupported without an appropriate source |

**Keep priority and evidence quality separate.** High-value, low-evidence requirements should remain visible as validation opportunities.

---

## 5. SMART generation is currently a hallucination risk

The plan says the system will generate quantified, testable specifications, but does not define how targets are grounded.

Customer complaints can support the need for improvement. They usually cannot establish:

- Exact latency thresholds.
- Existing architecture compatibility.
- Specific SOP dates.
- Package take-rate uplift.
- Detailed camera or hardware specifications.

Even the specification’s illustrative SMART example should not be treated as verified engineering evidence.

### Recommended requirement structure

Separate:

```text
Evidence-backed problem
Proposed customer-facing requirement
Proposed acceptance metric
Target provenance
Validation method
Feasibility assumptions
Target milestone and its provenance
```

A target can be:

- Source-backed.
- PM-entered.
- AI-proposed.
- Awaiting engineering validation.

For example:

> “Provide direct access to temperature adjustment with a proposed interaction target of no more than two actions, to be validated in a representative usability study.”

That is more defensible than inventing a component-level performance threshold.

Also distinguish **the need from the solution**. Difficult HVAC access might justify physical controls, a persistent digital shortcut, or improved voice interaction. Automatically selecting one implementation prematurely narrows the product decision.

---

## 6. The AI pipeline needs an actual execution design

The plan combines “deterministic engines” with clustering and generative SMART formulation. Those are different kinds of processing.

The deterministic parts should include:

- Counts and cohort denominators.
- Sales-volume calculations.
- Scoring.
- Status transitions.
- Evidence-link integrity.
- Audit verification.

The model-assisted parts should include:

- Topic/span extraction.
- Requirement drafting.
- Evidence synthesis.
- Alternatives and trade-off suggestions.

### A practical pipeline

```text
Import and preserve source data
    ↓
Canonicalize comments and retain annotations
    ↓
Group using existing categories plus semantic similarity
    ↓
Extract issue-specific spans and assign supporting/contradicting evidence
    ↓
Calculate counts deterministically
    ↓
Retrieve relevant surveys, equipment, and strategy passages
    ↓
Generate structured requirement drafts
    ↓
Validate citations, scope, targets, and required fields
    ↓
PM review
```

Important additions:

- Structured model outputs validated with Pydantic.
- Recorded model, prompt version, input references, and run ID.
- Cached responses and persisted embeddings.
- Bounded retries and visible failed/partial runs.
- An analysis-run endpoint/status screen; the current API list mostly exposes completed results.
- A clearly labeled cached mode for demo resilience.

Avoid making one model call per spreadsheet row. Existing annotations provide a strong starting point, and canonicalization reduces duplicated processing.

### Architecture recommendation

SQLite plus persisted embeddings and lexical search is sufficient at this scale. You can preserve relationship-based lineage without introducing a separate graph database.

The plan currently promises “GraphRAG” more than it defines a graph-based retrieval algorithm. Implement the retrieval behavior first; choose the label afterward.

---

## 7. Governance needs versioning and a real freeze operation

An ordinary `audit_log` table is not immutable or tamper-proof.

### Implement these together

**Versioned requirements**
- Each edit creates a new revision.
- Approval applies to a specific revision.
- Editing an approved requirement requires renewed approval.

**Transactional audit events**
- Requirement updates and audit events commit in the same transaction.
- Record actor, before/after state, rationale, and scoring configuration.
- AI generation events reference their analysis run.

**Tamper-evident ledger**
- Canonical event payloads.
- Previous-event hash and current-event hash.
- Verification included in export.

Be precise: a local hash chain detects modification relative to a trusted checkpoint, but a database administrator could rewrite the whole chain. An exported checkpoint strengthens the demonstration.

**G1 freeze snapshot**
- Approved requirement revisions.
- Evidence/source versions.
- Scoring weights and formula version.
- Accepted assumptions and unresolved issues.
- PM identity and timestamp.

Export should produce that snapshot, rather than simply dumping the current database.

### Other workflow corrections

- Opening a card should not automatically change its status to `UnderReview`.
- Align persisted states with the diagram: `Deferred` and `GateG1Candidate` are currently missing from the schema’s listed states.
- AI responses to a challenge should propose changes for review.
- Add revision checks to prevent one teammate silently overwriting another’s edit.
- Model market/powertrain scope explicitly; the API promises filters that the requirement schema does not adequately support.

---

## 8. Where to spend your extra AI capacity

I would prioritize substantive interactions over additional dashboard surfaces.

| Priority | Feature | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Essential | Evidence drawer with exact source locations | Proves traceability |
| Essential | Factor-by-factor score explanation | Proves decision logic |
| Essential | Edit/approve/reject with revision history | Proves human governance |
| Essential | Coverage gaps and unsupported-target labels | Proves trustworthy AI |
| Essential | Frozen G1 export | Completes the workflow |
| High value | Weight sensitivity and rank changes | Demonstrates trade-offs |
| High value | Regional requirement variants | Handles genuine market differences |
| High value | Structured “challenge this requirement” action | Makes AI useful during review |
| Stretch | Compare alternative solutions | Improves product decision quality |
| Lower value | Both Kanban and table, elaborate graph visualization | Adds UI work without much new evidence |

I would also remove “sentiment velocity” unless you obtain dated feedback. The supplied feedback headers do not include a timestamp.

For PDFs, ingest page-aware text broadly, then verify the specific equipment and strategy citations used by your showcase requirements. General-purpose extraction of every complex table is not necessary to establish real ingestion.

---

## 9. A realistic five-person delivery plan

The current roadmap is approximately **six hours of serial work**, with no ownership model and very little integration time. AI can accelerate coding, but data interpretation, contract mismatches, and citation validation remain bottlenecks.

### Suggested ownership

| Person | Primary ownership |
|---|---|
| **1 — Data/provenance** | Importers, canonical comments, annotations, survey/sales normalization, source references |
| **2 — AI/retrieval** | Signal extraction, retrieval, structured drafting, challenge action, caching |
| **3 — Backend/decision logic** | API contracts, scoring, revisions, audit chain, freeze/export; integration lead |
| **4 — Main PM UI** | Application shell, requirement table, editor, decisions, score explanation |
| **5 — Evidence/insight UI** | Evidence drawer, coverage/regional view, sensitivity UI; pitch and demo stewardship |

Have one owner for shared schema and contract changes, even if multiple people contribute.

### Schedule

| Time | Target |
|---|---|
| **0–0.75h** | Agree schema, status enums, source-reference format, API shapes, scoring rubric, and candidate demo cases |
| **0.75–3h** | Parallel build; deliver one real end-to-end requirement by hour 3 |
| **3–6h** | Integrate all source tiers, AI drafts, scoring, evidence, and decisions |
| **6–8.5h** | Add sensitivity, regional handling, challenge flow, revisions, and freeze/export |
| **8.5–10h** | Validate showcase evidence, fix integration issues, polish, prepare pitch |
| **10–12h** | Buffer, rehearsal, deployment/startup verification, stretch work only if stable |

**The key milestone is a vertical slice by hour 3:**

> Real feedback → signal → requirement → explained score → source evidence → PM decision → audit event.

### How to use agents effectively

Give agents bounded ownership and explicit interfaces:

- One importer or workbook normalization task.
- One UI component with a fixed response shape.
- One scoring module with mathematical invariants.
- One audit/export implementation.
- One validation task checking cited claims against sources.

Use separate branches/worktrees where appropriate. Avoid several agents simultaneously editing the shared schema, dependency configuration, or application shell.

---

## 10. Change the demo narrative

The proposed demo hard-codes complaint counts and a regional contradiction before validating them. Treat those as candidate scenarios.

Choose three evidence-backed requirements:

1. **Strong support:** recurring issue with relevant corroboration.
2. **Decision trade-off:** credible alternatives or genuinely conflicting signals.
3. **Evidence gap:** attractive proposal whose target or regional applicability needs validation.

Then demonstrate:

1. Discover a requirement.
2. Explain its score.
3. Open the original evidence.
4. Show an assumption or coverage gap.
5. Challenge or edit the proposal.
6. Approve the revised version with rationale.
7. Verify history and export the frozen G1 package.

A particularly strong moment would be:

> “The system has no evidence that Chinese customers prefer this interface. It identifies the gap and proposes validation before we commit to a regional variant.”

That directly answers BMW’s “we reward honesty” principle.

Measure business impact using observable prototype results—time to produce a cited draft, review time, traceability coverage—rather than claiming to compress the entire two-year planning process.

---

## Bottom line

**Proceed with the concept, but fix these before distributing implementation work:**

1. **Separate comments from annotation rows.**
2. **Replace the saturating scoring formula and expose factor provenance.**
3. **Distinguish regional conflicts from coverage gaps.**
4. **Label proposed SMART targets and feasibility assumptions explicitly.**
5. **Implement requirement revisions, transactional audit events, and a frozen G1 snapshot.**
6. **Build a real vertical slice early, then parallelize around stable contracts.**

With your team size and AI capacity, the cockpit, sensitivity simulation, challenge flow, and export are achievable. The strongest version will win through **defensible evidence and visible decision quality**, supported by a polished interface.

1: # BMW Product Management Challenge: Assignment Specification & Requirements Guide
2: 
3: **Challenge:** AI for Product Decision Making  
4: **Host:** BMW Group Product Management  
5: **Scope Focus:** Automotive Product Development Process — Steps 1 & 2 (Market Research & Product Planning to Gate G1 Concept Freeze)  
6: **Target Derivatives:** BMW 1 Series (F70), BMW 5 Series (G60/G68), BMW 7 Series (G70), and Future Successor Lines (Neue Klasse Architecture)  
7: **Target Markets:** Europe (EU), United States (US), China (CN), and Rest of World (RoW)  
8: 
9: ---
10: 
11: ## 1. Executive Summary & Mission Statement
12: 
13: Modern automotive product management requires synthesizing billions of fragmented market signals, customer reviews, warranty reports, competitor actions, and strategic corporate roadmaps into a coherent, customer-facing product specification. Today, this process spans approximately **two years** per vehicle generation and is predominantly manual, fragmented, and vulnerable to subjective bias.
14: 
15: ### The Mission
16: Develop an AI-powered, human-in-the-loop enterprise application that:
17: 1. **Ingests Heterogeneous Data**: Combines internal BMW customer feedback, quantitative satisfaction surveys, vehicle equipment catalogs, and strategic corporate reports.
18: 2. **Extracts Actionable Signals**: Discovers recurring complaints, unmet customer needs, competitor advantages, and emerging market trends, each strictly linked to originating evidence.
19: 3. **Derives SMART Product Requirements**: Formulates clear, customer-facing, realistic, and measurable requirements adhering to SMART criteria.
20: 4. **Prioritizes with Explainable Logic**: Applies an objective, transparent, multi-factor scoring methodology that balances customer value, regional volume impact, corporate strategy, and implementation complexity.
21: 5. **Keeps the Product Manager Firmly in the Loop**: Enables the PM to review, approve, reject, modify, or challenge requirements, rationales, and underlying evidence.
22: 6. **Maintains a Forensic Audit Trail**: Chronologically logs every system derivation, PM intervention, score override, and decision rationale to guarantee end-to-end governance.
23: 
24: ---
25: 
26: ## 2. Automotive Product Development Process Alignment
27: 
28: BMW management explicitly bounded the scope of this challenge to **Steps 1 and 2** of the 13-stage Automotive Product Development Lifecycle:
29: 
30: ```mermaid
31: flowchart TD
32:     subgraph Step1["Step 1: Market Research & Needs Analysis"]
33:         A1["Activities: Market Research, Customer Insights, Competitor Benchmarking, Trend Analysis"]
34:         A2["Deliverables: Market Opportunity Report, Customer Needs Document, Target Segments"]
35:         G0["Decision Gate: G0 — Project Approval"]
36:         A1 --> A2 --> G0
37:     end
38: 
39:     subgraph Step2["Step 2: Product Planning (Core App Focus)"]
40:         B1["Activities: Define Product Vision, Positioning, SMART Feature Prioritization, Trade-off Resolution"]
41:         B2["Deliverables: Product Plan, Project Charter, Prioritized Requirement List, Initial Business Sizing"]
42:         G1["Decision Gate: G1 — Concept Freeze"]
43:         B1 --> B2 --> G1
44:     end
45: 
46:     subgraph Step3["Steps 3 to 13: Concept to Continuous Feedback"]
47:         C1["G2 Feasibility -> G3 Design Freeze -> ... -> G9 SOP -> Step 13 Market Feedback Loop"]
48:     end
49: 
50:     Step1 --> Step2 --> Step3
51: 
52:     classDef default fill:#ffffff,stroke:#000000,color:#000000,stroke-width:1px;
53:     style Step1 fill:#ffffff,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#000000
54:     style Step2 fill:#ffffff,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:2px,color:#000000
55:     style Step3 fill:#ffffff,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#000000
56: ```
57: 
58: ### Boundary Definitions
59: * **In-Scope (Customer-Facing Product Attributes)**:
60:   * Interior comfort, ergonomics, and spatial packaging
61:   * Infotainment, operating system UX, and connected digital services
62:   * Climatization and thermal comfort controls
63:   * Driving experience and dynamic perception
64:   * Real-world charging UX and range perception
65:   * Equipment packaging, option bundling, and regional variant differentiation
66: * **Out-of-Scope**:
67:   * Regulatory and homologation compliance (e.g., UNECE safety, emissions type approval)
68:   * Low-level component specifications and supplier engineering schematics
69:   * Detailed unit economics, factory tooling capex, and bill-of-materials pricing calculations (rough implementation complexity/effort sizing is utilized as a prioritization factor)
70: 
71: ---
72: 
73: ## 3. Data Ecosystem & Inputs Profile
74: 
75: The application processes four distinct tiers of heterogeneous data:
76: 
77: ```
78: BMW-Data/
79: ├── F70_feedback_hackathon.xlsx              # 4,076 rows (1 Series - UK, JP, SE, FR)
80: ├── G60_feedback_hackathon.xlsx              # 5,005 rows (5 Series - US, KR, GB, JP, SE)
81: ├── G70_feedback_hackathon.xlsx              # 4,690 rows (7 Series - US, KR, JP, GB, CA)
82: ├── F70_G60_G68_G70_customer_studies.xlsx    # Quantitative satisfaction studies (China, EU, US)
83: ├── sales_volumes.xlsx                       # Market deliveries (2024, 2025, 2030 projections)
84: ├── F70_OptionList.PDF                       # Official German equipment catalog & packaging (1er)
85: ├── G60_OptionList.PDF                       # Official German equipment catalog & packaging (5er)
86: ├── G70_OptionList.PDF                       # Official German equipment catalog & packaging (7er)
87: └── BMW_Group_Report_2025.pdf / Q-Deck       # 400-page strategic corporate & financial report
88: ```
89: 
90: ### Dataset Characteristics
91: 
92: | Dataset | Volume | Key Attributes | Strategic Value |
93: | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
94: | **Customer Feedback** | 13,771 rows | `ID`, `Country`, `Engine Type` (ICE, BEV, PHEV), `Feedback Type` (Likes, DTU, Defect, Wants), `Customer Feedback`, `Vfc Category` | Voice of the customer; ground-truth operational friction, ergonomics, and feature desires. |
95: | **Customer Studies** | Quantitative sheets | Likert ratings (US) & Mean satisfaction scores (CN vs. EU) across 15 vehicle systems | Macro-level customer satisfaction benchmarks; correlates qualitative text with quantitative validation. |
96: | **Sales Volumes** | 4 regions $\times$ 3 vehicle lines | Volumes for 2024, 2025, and 2030 projections across EU, US, China, and RoW | Objective volume weighting factor for prioritization formulas. |
97: | **Option Catalogs** | 3 German PDFs | Standard vs. optional equipment, option codes, bundle packages (Innovation, Travel, Comfort) | Grounds proposed requirements in realistic production packaging. |
98: | **Strategic Report Deck** | ~400 pages | Neue Klasse platform roadmap, R&D priorities, BEV delivery targets, digital software KPIs | Strategic validation layer; ties customer desires to BMW engineering investments. |
99: 
100: ---
101: 
102: ## 4. Evaluation Criteria & Scoring Rubric
103: 
104: The challenge will be judged on five primary criteria, with one critical guiding principle:
105: 
106: | Dimension | Weight | Key Evaluation Requirements |
107: | :--- | :---: | :--- |
108: | **Decision & Scoring Logic** | 25% | Quality, consistency, and mathematical explainability of prioritization. Clear demonstration of how evidence sources are weighted and combined, and how trade-offs and conflicting signals are resolved. |
109: | **Workflow & Human Decision-Making** | 20% | Completeness of the end-to-end workflow from raw findings to prioritized requirements. Clearly defined roles, decision gates, and boundaries between autonomous AI and mandatory human review. |
110: | **Traceability & Auditability** | 20% | Full backward lineage from every requirement and score back to originating quotes, surveys, and report slides. Complete, chronological, tamper-evident audit history of all approvals, edits, and rejections. |
111: | **Solution Quality, Usability & Feasibility** | 20% | Prototype UI/UX polish, usability for BMW Product Managers and engineering peers, realistic applicability in an enterprise automotive environment, and quality of SMART formulations. |
112: | **Innovation, Scalability & Business Impact** | 15% | Originality of approach, cross-derivative scalability (F70 $\to$ G60 $\to$ G70 $\to$ Neue Klasse), reduction in manual requirement definition cycle time, and prevention of costly late-stage engineering rework. |
113: 
114: ### The Winning Differentiator: "We Reward Honesty"
115: > **Direct Quote from BMW Challenge Evaluation Criteria:**  
116: > *"We reward honesty. Trustworthy AI acknowledges uncertainty. Show us where your app lacks evidence, encounters conflicting signals, or reaches uncertain conclusions, and how this is surfaced to the PM. Honest limitations are a strength, not a weakness."*
117: 
118: The application must include an explicit **Uncertainty & Evidence Confidence Index** that transparently highlights:
119: 1. Low sample size / weak empirical support
120: 2. Regional contradictions (e.g., EU Autobahn driver desires vs. China chauffeur comfort)
121: 3. Extrapolations based on forward-looking assumptions (e.g., 2030 battery/software tech) versus proven historical data
122: 
123: ---
124: 
125: ## 5. SMART Requirements Framework
126: 
127: BMW requirements must strictly comply with the **SMART** standard:
128: 
129: | SMART Dimension | Definition | Automotive Context |
130: | :--- | :--- | :--- |
131: | **Specific** | Concrete and unambiguous system or feature scope | Exact UI component, sensor, or interior system |
132: | **Measurable** | Objective engineering/UX KPIs & thresholds | Clear quantifiable metrics (e.g. latency $< 45\text{ms}$, 60 fps) |
133: | **Attainable** | Feasible within vehicle architecture & manufacturing | Compatible with platform packaging & wiring harness |
134: | **Relevant** | Meaningfully solves verified customer pain | Directly resolves top complaint or aligns with brand strategy |
135: | **Timely** | Explicit SOP target & vehicle milestone | SOP 2028 (LCI / Successor / Neue Klasse milestone) |
136: 
137: ### Benchmark Example: From Complaint to SMART Requirement
138: * **Raw Voice of Customer (`G70-0891`)**: *"Customer noted she would have chosen the Home theater screen, but it obstructs the view out the rear and BMW does not offer a camera/rear-view mirror screen."*
139: * **Unacceptable Requirement (Vague)**: *"Improve rear visibility when the theater screen is down."*
140: * **SMART Requirement (`REQ-G70-VIS-001`)**:
141:   * **Specific**: Full-display digital streaming rear-view mirror system utilizing an aerodynamic roof-mounted wide-angle camera feeding directly into the central rear-view mirror.
142:   * **Measurable**: End-to-end video latency $< 45\text{ ms}$; frame rate $\ge 60\text{ fps}$ at $1080\text{p}$; dynamic range $> 120\text{ dB}$ (headlight anti-glare); camera lens auto-defrosting and wash nozzle operational from $-30^\circ\text{C}$ to $+65^\circ\text{C}$.
143:   * **Attainable**: Integrates with the existing Neue Klasse roof shark-fin camera housing and high-speed automotive Ethernet backbone.
144:   * **Relevant**: Eliminates the #1 safety blocker preventing theater screen adoption; projected to increase Theater Screen package take-rate by 18%.
145:   * **Timely**: Targeted for SOP 2028 (G70 LCI / Neue Klasse Luxury derivative).
146:   * **Package Strategy**: Standard on i7 M70; optional in Innovation Package for base derivatives.
147: 
148: ---
149: 
150: ## 6. Key Mentors & Stakeholder Insights
151: 
152: 1. **Bene_BMW (Product Management Pain Points)**:
153:    * *Cross-Market Regional Balancing*: Preferences differ radically by climate, usage habits, and culture. A single global specification often fails in either Europe, the US, or China.
154:    * *Predecessor Feedback Cycles*: Capturing field insights from outgoing models (e.g., F70, G60, G70) and projecting them 3–5 years ahead into future vehicle architectures.
155:    * *2-Year Timeline*: Requirement prioritization is not a one-time script; it is a collaborative, iterative governance process over ~24 months.
156: 2. **ThomasFremuthBMW**:
157:    * Ground proposals in real evidence; maintain strict data hygiene (do not commit raw internal data to public repositories).
158: 3. **Sebastian_BMW & ThomasBMW**:
159:    * Scope is tightly focused on Steps 1 & 2 of the automotive development framework.
160: 
161: ---
162: 
163: ## 7. Required Deliverables Checklist
164: 
165: - [ ] **Working Application Prototype**: Demonstrable full-stack software ingesting the datasets and providing an interactive PM experience.
166: - [ ] **Structured Sample Requirements List**: Complete table with Unique ID, SMART Description, Evidence Links, Priority Score, Evidence Level, Uncertainties, and Decision Status.
167: - [ ] **End-to-End Workflow Definition**: Clear division between AI autonomous analysis and mandatory PM decision gates.
168: - [ ] **Traceable & Reconstructable Audit Trail**: Forensic record of all requirement changes, score overrides, timestamps, actors, and documented rationales.
169: - [ ] **Pitch Presentation Deck (3–5 min)**: Compelling narrative demonstrating real-world value, data grounding, and Trustworthy AI principles.

(End of file - total 169 lines)
